final_message:
All five versions build with the provided scripts and print the exact expected output for every sample (s1, s2, s3), along with the other tests below.

## Algorithm (the same in all five)
1. **One pass over the input.** Each word is found, lowercased and hashed as it is read, then given a small integer id from an open-addressing hash table. The pass stores the sequence of word ids, with a flag on each word that starts a sentence. It also counts how many pairs begin with each word.
2. **Group the pairs by first word.** A counting sort on the first word puts the second word of every pair into that word's bucket.
3. **Count each group.** For each first word, its second words are counted in a plain array sized to the vocabulary. That array stays in the CPU cache, so there is no large hash table of pairs. This step also gives the distinct-pair count, and a small sorted list of 20 keeps the top pairs.
4. **Ties.** Before the top-20 step, the vocabulary (about 40k words) is sorted once to give each word a rank. Pairs with equal counts are then compared by rank numbers rather than by comparing strings.

My first C++ version stored every pair in a 64-bit-keyed hash table. It took 2.5 s and 255 MB on a 60 MB input. Most of that time was random memory access into the 128 MB table. The approach above brought it to about 0.7 s and 108 MB.

## Speed choices by language
- **C++:** Reads the file in one call into a buffer with zero padding at the end. It checks 8 bytes at a time to find where a word ends (a bit trick called SWAR, plus `countr_zero`) and hashes 8 bytes at a time. Each hash-table slot holds the word's first 8 lowercased bytes, so words shorter than 8 letters match with one integer compare. A new word is lowercased once, where it sits in the input. Other occurrences are compared with case folded and are never written back, which avoids a store-to-load stall I hit in an earlier version. Output is written in binary mode so lines end in `\n`, not `\r\n`.
- **Go:** Same design. It reads straight into one padded buffer (no second copy) and uses `encoding/binary` loads and `math/bits`.
- **C#:** Same design, using `unsafe` pointers, `Unsafe.ReadUnaligned`, `BitOperations` and arrays allocated without zero-filling. In `solution.csproj` I added `TieredCompilation=false`, so the main loop is fully compiled from the start, and switched off the concurrent and server garbage collectors.
- **Java:** Same design, using a `VarHandle` to read 8 bytes at a time. Each slot's prefix, hash and id share one `long[]` so a lookup touches one place in memory. The file is read through `FileChannel` into a padded array. The id array starts small and grows, because Java zero-fills every new array.
- **JavaScript:** JavaScript has no cheap 64-bit integers, so this version reads a byte at a time with a 32-bit `Math.imul` hash. All tables are typed arrays (`Int32Array`), and a negative id marks a word that starts a sentence. Strings are built only for sorting the vocabulary and for the output.

## Results
| | samples s1–s3 | extra tests (10) | 60 MB input |
|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | pass | pass | ~0.6–0.9 s, 108 MB |
| Go | pass | pass | ~0.75–1.25 s, 114 MB |
| C# | pass | pass | ~0.75 s, 132 MB |
| Java | pass | pass | ~1.3 s, 236 MB |
| JS | pass | pass | ~1.4–1.8 s, 152 MB |

The 10 extra tests cover:
- an empty file
- punctuation only
- a single word
- fewer than 20 pairs
- 200k mostly-distinct words, so all counts tie and the hash table has to grow
- long mixed-case words that differ only after byte 8 or byte 16
- a 5 MB and a 60 MB generated input

I checked every result against a separate Python reference that also matches the samples. The machine was about 80% busy with other work during these runs, so the times are rough. Java's memory figure is mostly the JVM's default heap.

The test scripts are in `testtools/`, including a 60 MB `big.in` you may want to delete.

request.prompt:
You are writing five versions of the same program, in C++, Java, C#, Go and JavaScript, for a comparison of
how fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Each language has its own folder with a starting file and a `build.cmd`. The benchmark builds every program with
these same build scripts and flags, whatever you change in them. Write these programs:

1. `cpp/main.cpp` (more `.cpp` and header files in `cpp/` are fine): C++20, built by `cpp\build.cmd` with
   Microsoft Visual C++ 19.40 (Visual Studio 2022) and `/O2 /GL /EHsc /std:c++20`. Standard library only, plus
   nlohmann/json 3.12 (`#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>`, already in `cpp/include/`). Run as
   `cpp\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
2. `java/src/Main.java` (more `.java` files in `java/src/` are fine): Java 23, built by `java\build.cmd` with
   `javac`. Java SE only, plus Jackson 2.22 (core, databind and annotations, already in `java/lib/`). Run as
   `java\run.cmd INPUT_PATH`, which runs `java -cp "out;lib\*" Main` with the default JVM settings.
3. `csharp/Program.cs` (more `.cs` files in `csharp/` are fine): C# 12 on .NET 8, built in Release by
   `csharp\build.cmd`. Base class library only. You may change properties in `csharp/solution.csproj`, but do not
   add package references. Run as `csharp\out\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
4. `go/main.go` (more `.go` files in `go/` are fine): Go 1.27, built by `go\build.cmd`. Standard library only.
   Run as `go\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
5. `js/main.js`: JavaScript on Node.js 22, with no build step. Built-in Node modules only; no npm packages. Run as
   `node js\main.js INPUT_PATH`.

Each program reads the input file whose path is its first argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments) and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input. Python 3.13 (`C:\Python313\python.exe`) is
available if you want it for testing, but not as part of any program.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Build and test all five versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside
this folder, and take at most about 60 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time: never stop
a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example `taskkill /IM java.exe` or
`Stop-Process -Name node`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
